deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivations. It holds aphoristic, philosophical-pedagogical notes from Hilbert's notebook series of 'Allgemein Mathematisch-Philosophische Bemerkungen'. There are four separate entries, divided by horizontal rules.

(0) Continuation of the Moltke analogy. The opening fragment ('[Mancher] Gemeine wird von seinem Feldherrn gering denken, wenn er schlecht schiesst ...') finishes the question 'Soll Moltke die Schiessübungen mitmachen? Mancher' that ends the page supplied as 'next'. So in the physical sequence that page precedes this one, or the excerpt order is scrambled.
- The point: the field marshal (the general idea-bearer) need not master rifle practice (technical detail).
- Yet for the 'moral' reason of keeping the respect of the common soldier, it is in fact useful if he can shoot well.
- Applied to mathematics: the leading mind should command technique too, if only for authority. This ties to the previous page's remark that every skill is useful, even swimming for mathematicians, and the only question is whether acquiring it pays.

(1) Word versus thought: invariance under change of representation.
- The spoken word (its sound, 'Ton') is inessential.
- It can be replaced by any other sign system: conventional ones (cipher, telegraph codes) or historically fixed or agreed ones.
- Only the thought stays the same; Hilbert calls it 'die Invariante'.
- In modern terms: meaning is what is invariant under the group of recodings (bijective substitutions of the sign system). This is a semiotic analogue of the invariant-theoretic viewpoint, and close in spirit to his later formalist and axiomatic stance that the names of primitive terms are interchangeable.

(2) The garden-woman question.
- Does a gardener know better what a plane is because she can level ground ('planiren') more surely?
- Does she know better what a straight line is because she can stake out the paths on a vegetable bed exactly?
- Does she know better what is continuously curved because she draws the curved path lines more surely?
- Implied answer: no. Practical or manual skill is not conceptual geometric knowledge.
- This targets the claim, debated in school-reform discussions of the time (e.g. in Klein's circle), that drawing and handicraft build geometric intuition.

(3) Different interests in the same object.
- Anecdote: a railway companion, a cloth salesman, did not know Göttingen. Only after a while did he ask whether it was the place near Weende (a village just north of Göttingen), i.e. an inversion of importance.
- A statistician might care whether the letter 'a' occurs an even or odd number of times in Sophocles' Antigone, or whether more tragedies have an even or odd number of verses (marginal addition: 'oder Reimzahl', or of rhymes).
- The point: the same object carries entirely different 'interesting' features depending on viewpoint. Parity counts are meaningless invariants for literature.

(4) Start of a new entry, continued overleaf: 'Does geometric drawing train geometric intuition so much? and not rather ...'. The previous page supplies the continuation ('das freihändige Zeichnen? ...'), which again suggests the folio order is reversed relative to the 'previous/next' labels.

results.what: Remark that the thought expressed by a word is the invariant under arbitrary conventional recodings of the sign (cipher, telegraph code), the sound of the word being inessential
results.modern_name: Meaning as invariant under change of representation (semiotic/structuralist view; analogy to invariant theory)
results.usually_credited_to: General philosophical theme (Frege, Saussure, etc.); Hilbert's formalism is often illustrated by his 'tables, chairs, beer mugs' remark (c. 1891, reported by Blumenthal)

results.modern_name: Distinction between practical skill and conceptual/axiomatic geometric knowledge (pedagogy of geometric intuition)
results.usually_credited_to: Contemporary debates on mathematics education (Klein's reform movement), Hilbert's own lectures on Anschauung

deep.surprise_reason: These are personal philosophical aphorisms. The remark calling the thought 'die Invariante' under change of sign system is a nice, quotable anticipation of Hilbert's formalist view that the choice of symbols and names is immaterial. That view is already well documented as his, so the page is of biographical and intellectual-historical interest but not a new mathematical result.
